source.title: The Generalization-Stability Tradeoff in Neural Network Pruning
source.authors: Brian R. Bartoldson; Ari S. Morcos; Adrian Barbu; G. Erlebacher

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full paper, including appendices; no truncation or garbling that prevents extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests how pruning interventions and measured pruning stability relate to test accuracy and the train–test gap using pruning/noise experiments, rather than testing the claim's listed original recipes directly.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper's own pruning and noise interventions and its stability/flatness measurements. Cited results about overparameterized networks fitting randomized data and other prior work are not rows. Figure-only comparisons without a text-stated numeric value are recorded as figure-only.
record.test_reason: The study measures pruning instability, temporary parameter noise, and unscaled flatness measures. None tests V1–V8. In particular, its flatness analysis uses test-loss curvature and absolute parameter perturbations, whereas V7 specifies magnitude-scaled perturbations measured by increases in training error. Dropout analogies and citations to width and memorization results do not constitute tests.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that pruning instability can improve generalization within a useful range, that permanent parameter removal is unnecessary for these benefits, and that noise-induced flatness offers a possible mechanism. The flatness evidence is correlational; pruning does not consistently improve on the unpruned baseline.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies structured magnitude pruning and pruning-like noise during training; the claim versions focus on random-label fitting, width, architecture, optimizers, batches, dropout, sharpness measures, or memorized-example removal.
record.method_sensitivity: Pruning stability and generalization depend on pruning target, iterative pruning rate, total pruning percentage, model architecture, optimizer/training setup, data augmentation, and dataset. The generalization benefit weakens or reverses when pruning is already too unstable; the benefit of instability also varies with the training regularization regime.

fits_no_version.finding: Lower pruning stability correlates with higher test accuracy and smaller generalization gaps in several image classifiers, with benefits weakening or reversing at excessive instability. Under the standard training setup, Figure 4's pruned models did not outperform the unpruned baseline on average.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Structured pruning has a stability-dependent regularization effect whose useful range depends on the training recipe.

fits_no_version.finding: Temporary filter zeroing and sufficiently prolonged Gaussian parameter noise reproduce some pruning-related accuracy gains without requiring permanent parameter removal.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pruning-like parameter noise can improve generalization without permanently reducing model capacity.

fits_no_version.finding: Test-loss curvature, gradient covariance, absolute eigenvector perturbation tolerance, and a TIC proxy correlate with pruning stability or test accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unscaled flatness and noise-sensitivity measures correlate with generalization across pruning configurations in VGG11 on CIFAR-10.

record.peer_reviewed: NeurIPS 2020 (34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems; supplied venue metadata says 2019)
record.problems: Several reported comparisons are conveyed by figures without exact values in the text; the standard-training experiments use limited pruning configurations, and the CIFAR-100 table has only three runs per configuration. The study's proposed flatness mechanism is correlational.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports additional results and plots in Figures B.2, C.1–C.3, D.2, E.1–E.6 and Tables C.1 and F.1. Rows were not added for every appendix variant, duplicate correlation plot, or figure-only trajectory because the central outcomes and distinct conditions are captured above; exact values not stated in text remain figure-only or are omitted.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, natural-label held-out accuracy, and chance-level random-label held-out accuracy under matched training recipes.
Widening beyond the width required for zero training error and measuring subsequent test-error changes.
Convolutional versus fully connected classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Controlled adaptive-optimizer versus SGD comparisons under specified tuning budgets.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Dropout addition or removal, training-set-size dependence, and excessive-dropout underfitting.
Magnitude-scaled weight perturbations evaluated using training error, their relationship to generalization gaps, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized training examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: All rows retain versions ["none"]. Their cannot_determine states indicate that their measures cannot establish an effect specified by V1–V8, not that the reported pruning findings are unreadable or absent. Appendix F invokes prior width results but supplies no width sweep. No additional result testing a listed version was found in the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Adaptive optimizer versus SGD generalization comparison.
Dropout addition/removal and its effect on test error.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring resulting accuracy.

rows.subject: VGG11
rows.stage_stated: trained on CIFAR-10 with Adam for 325 epochs; no data augmentation
rows.operation_detail: Pruned filters with PruneL and compared against temporary zeroing noise applied for 50 consecutive training batches.
rows.measure: Test accuracy during training and at the end
rows.baseline: No Noise and PruneL are plotted as comparisons; numeric baseline not stated
rows.value: Zeroing 50 has strikingly similar final generalization performance to PruneL; similar instability and test accuracy throughout training
rows.uncertainty: 10 runs; 95% confidence intervals for means, bootstrapped
rows.note: Temporary zeroing is applied to filters instead of permanently pruning them.
rows.check: Magnitude-targeted filter zeroing over consecutive batches is a pruning-like intervention, not a test of configured dropout in V6.
